A small routine with a week of practice

How every teacher guide works

  1. SHOW. Do the first action and read the SAY line aloud.
  2. TRY. Give students the stated action. Pair students seated beside each other.
  3. CHECK. Listen for the supplied answer. Use If students get stuck when needed.

Times are a guide. Pause and repeat a step when students need more practice. Keep the grade-level content goal; adjust access, language, and practice.

Research foundation

What reading science means here: complementary strands of instruction, chosen for the learner and the task.

Word reading + language understanding

Students need accurate word recognition and an understanding of the language and ideas in text. The National Reading Panel synthesized evidence on sound awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. Its 2000 report is a historical foundation, not a current EL-specific curriculum.

English learners need explicit language teaching

The IES English learner guide recommends sustained vocabulary instruction and integrating oral and written language with content. It also addresses structured writing and targeted small-group support. Its direct scope is elementary and middle school; high-school uses in this binder are adaptations.

Adolescents need meaning and word access

The adolescent literacy guide supports explicit vocabulary and comprehension instruction, text discussion, engagement, and specialist intervention when needed. The grades 4–9 intervention guide addresses multisyllabic decoding, fluency, comprehension, and supported challenging text.

Writing helps students make thinking visible

The secondary writing guide recommends explicit strategy modeling, practice, and reflection; connecting reading and writing; and using writing samples to inform instruction. Evidence strength differs across these recommendations.

What is original in this binder

The titles, scripts, cartoons, practice missions, examples, and language lanes are original classroom applications of those recommendations. They have not been evaluated as a 36-week program. A source tag connects a move to a broader practice; it does not establish that the exact move or five-minute dose has a measured effect.

Teacher decisions

Use supports with precision. Language proficiency, literacy experience, and content knowledge can develop differently.

Choose by the task

The three lanes describe current support needs: newcomer/access, emerging/scaffolded language, and progressing/greater independence. These are flexible teaching choices, not official ELPA21 score assignments. Offer an extension when useful; never lower the shared content goal.

Use visuals to explain

Pair an accurate, uncluttered sketch, diagram, or data display with its written labels and spoken explanation. Point explicitly between them. Labels and shapes should remain meaningful in grayscale.

Build from students' languages

Invite bilingual planning, verified translations, and useful cognates when they help students express content. Home-language supports are optional; never assume every student speaks Spanish or reads their home language.

Teach word reading directly when needed

Pictures and context help explain meaning, but students identify printed words through their spelling. A sound or word-part preview is not a full phonics sequence. If word reading is persistently difficult, involve the EL teacher and reading specialist.

Separate access from the skill measured

Read-aloud can open access to demanding content. It does not show what a student can decode independently. Note the supports used. Accent alone does not indicate a reading problem.

Respond to actual performance

Keep required accommodations. Fade temporary prompts only after successful use. Brief classroom checks guide next steps; they do not diagnose a disability or establish English proficiency.

Evidence map

What the references support

Recommendation numbers on the move cards (e.g., R2:2) refer to these source families.

Read the ratings carefully

Strong, moderate, and minimal are the guides' ratings for broad recommendations. Minimal evidence is not evidence of no benefit. None of these ratings transfers automatically to a particular board model, language lane, weekly order, or five-minute routine in this binder.

Scope and use

This binder emphasizes Tier 1 content access and brief literacy practice. It is not a screening instrument, a comprehensive phonics curriculum, or a substitute for EL services and individualized reading intervention. Teachers should coordinate with their EL and reading specialists.

For a faculty meeting: Read one recommendation together, model a move with an actual lesson text, and compare what students produce. Choose the next move from evidence of need rather than from the calendar alone.
